courses.title: Active Directory Deep Dive
courses.description: Master Active Directory Domain Services end to end — architecture, domains and forests, OUs, groups, FSMO roles, replication, trusts, and health maintenance.

content.intro: Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is the identity backbone of a Windows network — it stores objects (users, computers, groups) and authenticates and authorises access across the domain.

ul.t: the top-level security boundary that contains one or more domains sharing a schema and global catalog.
an administrative and replication boundary for objects and policy.
the blueprint defining every object class and attribute — one schema per forest.
a partial, forest-wide index that speeds searches and logons.

p: A domain controller (DC) is a server running the AD DS role that holds a writable copy of the domain database (NTDS.dit) and authenticates users. Best practice is at least two DCs per domain for redundancy.
You add the AD DS role, then promote the server to a domain controller (creating a new forest, new domain, or additional DC).

ul.t: the AD database file on each DC.
a replicated share holding scripts and Group Policy files.

note.text: Promoting the first DC in a new domain also typically installs DNS — AD depends on DNS to locate services via SRV records.

content.practice: In a lab, install the AD DS role and promote a server to the first domain controller of a new forest 'lab.local'. Confirm DNS was installed and the SYSVOL share exists.

quiz.p: What is the top-level security boundary in Active Directory?
quiz.ex: The forest is the top-level security boundary; it contains domains sharing a schema.

quiz.p: Which file is the Active Directory database on a domain controller?
quiz.ex: NTDS.dit stores the directory database on each DC.

quiz.p: AD DS depends on which service to locate domain controllers?
quiz.ex: Clients find DCs via DNS SRV records, so AD requires DNS.

content.intro: Larger organisations structure Active Directory into multiple domains, trees, and forests. Understanding these relationships is key to designing and supporting an enterprise directory.

p: A tree is one or more domains sharing a contiguous DNS namespace (e.g. corp.example.com and sales.corp.example.com). A forest can hold multiple trees with different namespaces, all trusting each other automatically.
Domain and forest functional levels determine which AD features are available and set a minimum DC operating system. Raise them only once all DCs meet the requirement — it cannot be easily reversed.

ul: Separate administrative or password policies (historically)
Replication control across slow WAN links
Regulatory or organisational separation

note.text: Modern designs favour a single domain with OUs for delegation, rather than many domains — simpler and cheaper to run.

p: All domains in a forest trust each other through automatic, transitive, two-way trusts, so a user in one domain can be granted access to resources in another.

content.practice: Diagram your organisation (or a fictional one) as a forest: name the forest root domain, any child domains, and note the functional level you would target.

quiz.p: Domains in the same forest trust each other via…
quiz.ex: Intra-forest trusts are automatic, two-way, and transitive.

quiz.p: A contiguous DNS namespace of parent/child domains forms a…
quiz.ex: A tree is domains sharing a contiguous namespace.

quiz.p: Raising the forest functional level primarily…
o: Enables newer AD features and sets a minimum DC OS
quiz.ex: Functional levels gate features and require a minimum DC OS.

content.intro: Organizational Units (OUs) are containers that structure a domain for management — they are where you apply Group Policy and delegate administrative control.

p: Unlike the default containers (like Users), OUs can have Group Policy linked to them and support delegation. Design OUs around how you administer objects, not just the org chart.
The Delegation of Control Wizard grants specific rights (e.g. reset passwords, create users) over an OU to a group — enabling least-privilege administration without handing out Domain Admin.

ul.t: the OU hierarchy by default.
stops inherited GPOs at an OU (use sparingly).

ul: Keep the structure shallow and logical
Separate users, computers, and service accounts
Name OUs consistently

note.text: You can't apply Group Policy to a default container — put objects into OUs to manage them with GPOs.

content.practice: Create an OU structure for a small company (e.g. OUs for Staff, Workstations, Servers, ServiceAccounts) and delegate 'reset password' rights on the Staff OU to a Helpdesk group.

quiz.p: What can you do with an OU that you cannot do with a default container?
o: Link Group Policy and delegate control
quiz.ex: OUs support GPO links and delegation; default containers do not.

quiz.p: The Delegation of Control Wizard is used to…
o: Grant specific admin rights over an OU
quiz.ex: It grants scoped rights to a group for least-privilege admin.

quiz.p: By default, GPOs and permissions on a parent OU…
quiz.ex: Inheritance flows settings down the OU hierarchy.

content.intro: Groups are how you grant access at scale. Choosing the right group type and scope — and following a consistent nesting strategy — keeps permissions manageable.

ul.t: grant access to resources (used in permissions).
email lists only, no security use.
used to assign permissions to resources in its own domain.
groups users from its own domain by role.
spans domains across the forest (stored in the global catalog).

p: Best practice: put Accounts into Global groups, Global groups into Domain Local groups, and assign Permissions to the Domain Local group (A-G-DL-P). It keeps access clean and auditable.

note.text: Grant access through groups, never to individual users — it scales and is far easier to audit and revoke.

content.practice: Design access to a shared folder using AGDLP: create a Global group for a role (e.g. 'GG_Sales'), a Domain Local group for the resource (e.g. 'DL_SalesShare_Modify'), nest one in the other, and assign the folder permission to the Domain Local group.

quiz.p: Which group type is used to assign resource permissions?
quiz.ex: Security groups are used in permissions; distribution groups are for email.

quiz.p: In the AGDLP strategy, permissions are assigned to which group?
quiz.ex: Accounts→Global→Domain Local→Permissions: permissions go on the Domain Local group.

quiz.p: A Global group is best used to…
o: Group users by role in their domain
quiz.ex: Global groups collect users by role; Domain Local groups get the permissions.

content.intro: Most AD operations are multi-master, but five Flexible Single Master Operations (FSMO) roles must be held by exactly one DC each to avoid conflicts.

ul.t: the only DC that can change the schema.
adds/removes domains in the forest.
hands out pools of relative IDs so SIDs stay unique.
time source, password changes, account lockout, and GPO editing point.
maintains cross-domain object references.

p: Two forest-wide roles (Schema, Domain Naming) sit on one DC in the forest root. The three domain roles exist once per domain. The PDC Emulator is the most impactful — keep it on a reliable DC.

ul.t: gracefully move a role when both DCs are online (preferred).
force-assign a role when the holder is permanently dead — never bring the old holder back afterward.

note.text: Seizing a role from a DC that later returns causes serious corruption. Only seize when the original is gone for good.

content.practice: List which DC holds each FSMO role in a lab (netdom query fsmo), then practice transferring the PDC Emulator role to another DC and back.

quiz.p: Which FSMO role is the authoritative time source and handles account lockouts?
quiz.ex: The PDC Emulator is the time source and central point for lockouts and password changes.

quiz.p: How many DCs can hold the Schema Master role in a forest?
quiz.ex: Schema Master is a single forest-wide role held by exactly one DC.

quiz.p: You should 'seize' a FSMO role only when…
o: The current holder is permanently offline
quiz.ex: Seize only when the holder is gone for good; otherwise transfer gracefully.

content.intro: Active Directory replicates changes between all domain controllers. Sites and subnets tell AD about your physical network so it can replicate and direct clients efficiently.

p: A site represents a well-connected physical location; you associate IP subnets with sites so clients authenticate against a nearby DC and replication respects WAN links.

ul.t: fast, uncompressed, change-notification based (near real-time).
scheduled and compressed over site links to save bandwidth.

p: The Knowledge Consistency Checker (KCC) automatically builds and maintains the replication topology, creating connection objects between DCs.

note.text: Every writable DC accepts changes and replicates them out; conflicts are resolved by version numbers and timestamps.

content.practice: Create a second site and a site link in a lab, associate a subnet with it, and use repadmin /replsummary to review replication health.

quiz.p: Associating IP subnets with sites lets clients…
o: Authenticate against a nearby domain controller
quiz.ex: Subnet-to-site mapping directs clients to a local DC.

quiz.p: Inter-site replication is…
o: Scheduled and compressed over site links
quiz.ex: Inter-site replication is compressed and scheduled to conserve WAN bandwidth.

quiz.p: Which component builds the replication topology automatically?
quiz.ex: The Knowledge Consistency Checker (KCC) maintains connection objects.

content.intro: Trusts let users in one domain or forest access resources in another. Knowing the trust types and their direction and transitivity is essential for cross-organisation access.

ul.t: one-way or two-way (who can access whom).
transitive trusts extend to trusted-by-the-trusted domains; non-transitive don't.
automatic, transitive, within a forest.
non-transitive trust to a single domain in another forest.
trust between two whole forests (transitive across them).
speeds authentication between two domains deep in a forest.
to a non-Windows Kerberos realm.

p: Forest trusts are common in mergers, letting users in Forest A access resources in Forest B while each keeps its own administration.

content.practice: In a lab (or on paper), decide which trust type you'd use to let a partner company's forest access one of your file servers, and note its direction and transitivity.

quiz.p: A forest trust between two forests is…
o: The same as a shortcut trust
quiz.ex: Forest trusts are transitive across the two forests.

quiz.p: An external trust is…
quiz.ex: External trusts are non-transitive, to one domain in another forest.

quiz.p: A shortcut trust is used to…
o: Speed authentication between two domains in a forest
quiz.ex: Shortcut trusts shorten the referral path between domains in a forest.

content.intro: A healthy directory needs monitoring, backup, and occasional cleanup. These are the tools and tasks that keep AD reliable.

ul.t: runs a battery of DC health tests.
reports and troubleshoots replication.

p: Back up System State on DCs. To recover deleted objects, enable the AD Recycle Bin; for authoritative restores, boot into Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) and use ntdsutil.

ul.t: offline defrag, metadata cleanup, and snapshots.
removes remnants of a DC that was not demoted cleanly.

note.text: Keep time in sync (the PDC Emulator is the root source) — Kerberos fails if clocks drift more than a few minutes.

content.practice: Run dcdiag and repadmin /replsummary against a lab DC, then enable the AD Recycle Bin and recover a test user you deleted.

quiz.p: Which tool reports domain controller health tests?
quiz.ex: dcdiag runs DC health diagnostics.

quiz.p: The AD Recycle Bin lets you…
quiz.ex: It restores deleted AD objects with their attributes.

quiz.p: Kerberos authentication fails if clocks between hosts drift more than about…
quiz.ex: By default a skew beyond ~5 minutes breaks Kerberos, so time sync matters.

courses.title: Group Policy Mastery
courses.description: Control Windows at scale with Group Policy — architecture, processing order, security settings, preferences, deployment, and troubleshooting.

content.intro: Group Policy centrally configures users and computers. Knowing how a GPO is built and stored explains how settings actually reach a machine.

ul.t: applies to the machine at startup and refresh.
applies to the user at logon and refresh.
the object in AD (metadata, version).
the files in SYSVOL (the actual settings).

p: A GPO takes effect only when linked to a site, domain, or OU. One GPO can be linked in multiple places; edits apply everywhere it's linked.

note.text: Policy applies at startup/logon and refreshes roughly every 90 minutes (with a random offset) — or immediately with gpupdate.

content.practice: In the Group Policy Management Console, create a GPO, note its GUID, and find the matching folder under \\domain\SYSVOL. Link it to a test OU.

quiz.p: A GPO takes effect when it is…
o: Linked to a site, domain, or OU
quiz.ex: An unlinked GPO does nothing; linking to a container applies it.

quiz.p: The actual policy files are stored in…
quiz.ex: The Group Policy Template lives in SYSVOL; the GPC is the AD object.

quiz.p: By default, Group Policy refreshes in the background about every…
quiz.ex: Background refresh is ~90 minutes with a random offset.

content.intro: When multiple GPOs apply, the order they process determines who wins. This is the single most important thing to understand for predictable results.

p: GPOs process Local, then Site, then Domain, then OU (deepest last). Later wins, so the OU closest to the object generally takes precedence on conflicting settings.

ul.t: among GPOs on one container, lower link order number wins.
forces a GPO to win and prevents it being blocked.
stops inherited GPOs at an OU (Enforced overrides this).

p: A GPO applies only to users/computers with Read and Apply permissions — use security filtering to target specific groups.

note.text: Loopback processing applies user settings based on the computer's location — common for kiosks and shared machines.

content.practice: Create two GPOs with a conflicting setting, link both to an OU, and use link order + Enforced to control which one wins. Verify with gpresult.

quiz.p: The default GPO processing order is…
quiz.ex: LSDOU: Local, Site, Domain, OU — later (OU) wins on conflicts.

quiz.p: An 'Enforced' GPO link…
o: Wins and cannot be blocked by inheritance
quiz.ex: Enforced forces precedence and overrides Block Inheritance.

quiz.p: Security filtering lets you…
o: Target a GPO to specific users/computers
quiz.ex: Filtering scopes a GPO to objects with Apply permission.

content.intro: Group Policy's most common job is enforcing security baselines. These settings harden every machine consistently.

p: Set at the domain level: minimum password length, complexity, lockout threshold, and duration. In modern AD, fine-grained password policies can target specific groups.

ul.t: who can log on locally, as a service, etc.
what security events are logged (logons, object access).

p: Thousands of registry-backed settings (ADMX files) control Windows and app behaviour — from screen lock timeouts to disabling features.

note.text: Start from Microsoft's Security Baselines rather than hand-building policy — then tailor.

content.practice: Create a GPO that enforces a screen-lock timeout and an audit policy for logon events; link it to a test OU and confirm it applies.

quiz.p: Password complexity and lockout are typically set…
quiz.ex: Account policies apply at the domain level (with fine-grained exceptions).

quiz.p: Administrative Templates are backed by…
quiz.ex: Admin templates map to registry values defined in ADMX files.

quiz.p: A good starting point for hardening policy is…
quiz.ex: Security Baselines give a vetted starting configuration.

content.intro: Group Policy Preferences (GPP) configure things that aren't strict 'policy' — like mapped drives, printers, and registry keys — with powerful targeting.

ul: Map network drives
Deploy printers
Set registry values and environment variables
Create shortcuts and files

p: Policies are enforced and re-applied; preferences set an initial state a user can often change. Preferences are ideal for defaults.
Each preference can be filtered by OS, group membership, IP range, and more — so one GPO can apply different settings to different targets.

note.text: Never store passwords in GPP — historically they were recoverable. Microsoft removed that capability for good reason.

content.practice: Create a GPP that maps a network drive only for members of a specific security group using item-level targeting.

quiz.p: Group Policy Preferences are best for…
o: Setting defaults like mapped drives and printers
quiz.ex: Preferences configure things like drives and printers, often user-changeable.

quiz.p: Item-level targeting lets a single preference…
o: Apply to specific OSes, groups, or IP ranges
quiz.ex: Targeting filters which objects receive the preference.

quiz.p: You should never use GPP to store…
quiz.ex: GPP password storage was insecure and has been removed.

content.intro: Group Policy can redirect user folders to the network and install software automatically — two classic enterprise capabilities.

p: Redirect Documents, Desktop, and other known folders to a network share so data is centralised, backed up, and follows the user between machines.

ul.t: installs at startup for all users of the machine.
installs at logon or on demand.

p: GPSI deploys Windows Installer (.msi) packages. For anything more complex, most organisations now use dedicated tools (Intune, Configuration Manager).

note.text: Folder redirection pairs well with Offline Files so users keep working when the share is unavailable.

content.practice: Configure folder redirection for Documents to a share for a test OU, and note how you would assign an .msi to computers via GPO.

quiz.p: Folder redirection is used to…
o: Point user folders like Documents to a network share
quiz.ex: It redirects known folders to a central, backed-up location.

quiz.p: Assigning software to a computer via GPO installs it…
o: At startup for all users of that machine
quiz.ex: Computer-assigned software installs at startup for the machine.

quiz.p: GPO software installation (GPSI) deploys which package type?
quiz.ex: GPSI deploys .msi packages; complex apps use other tools.

content.intro: When a policy 'isn't applying,' a short set of tools tells you exactly what happened and why.

ul.t: reapply policy immediately.
a Resultant Set of Policy report showing what applied and what was filtered.

ul: The GPO isn't linked to the right OU
Security filtering excludes the object
Block Inheritance or precedence is overriding it
SYSVOL/replication problems

p: If DCs disagree, clients may get old settings. Check SYSVOL replication (DFSR) and AD replication with repadmin.

note.text: Some settings are skipped over slow links, and loopback can explain 'wrong' user settings on shared machines.

content.practice: Run gpresult /h on a test machine, identify one GPO that was filtered out and why, then fix the cause and re-verify.

quiz.p: Which command produces a Resultant Set of Policy report?
quiz.ex: gpresult /h writes an HTML RSoP report of applied policy.

quiz.p: A GPO applies but a user still doesn't get it — a likely cause is…
quiz.ex: Security filtering (Apply permission) commonly blocks application.

quiz.p: Disagreeing DCs handing out old policy points to a problem with…
quiz.ex: Replication issues cause inconsistent policy delivery.

courses.title: DNS & DHCP In Depth
courses.description: Run the two services every Windows network depends on — authoritative DNS (zones, records, forwarding, security) and DHCP (scopes, high availability, troubleshooting).

content.intro: DNS resolves names to addresses and locates services. On Windows Server, you host authoritative zones that answer for your namespace.

ul.t: name → IP (the common case).
IP → name (PTR records).
the writable master copy.
a read-only copy via zone transfer.
stored in AD, multi-master, replicated with the directory — the recommended choice on DCs.

p: AD-integrated zones give fault tolerance (every DC can answer and update), secure dynamic updates, and replication for free.

note.text: Secure dynamic updates (AD-integrated only) stop rogue clients from registering or hijacking records.

content.practice: Create a forward and a reverse lookup zone on a lab DC as AD-integrated, and enable secure dynamic updates.

quiz.p: A reverse lookup zone resolves…
quiz.ex: Reverse zones map IPs back to names via PTR records.

quiz.p: The recommended zone type on a domain controller is…
quiz.ex: AD-integrated zones are multi-master, replicated, and support secure updates.

quiz.p: Secure dynamic updates require which zone type?
quiz.ex: Only AD-integrated zones support secure dynamic updates.

content.intro: Each record type answers a different question. Recognising them is essential for both configuration and troubleshooting.

ul.t: host name to IPv4 / IPv6 address.
an alias to another name.
mail server for a domain.
reverse (IP to name).
locates services — how clients find domain controllers.
delegation and zone authority/parameters.
free text — SPF, DKIM, verification.

note.text: AD publishes SRV records so clients can find DCs, global catalog, and Kerberos — which is why broken DNS breaks logons.

content.practice: In a lab, create an A record and a CNAME alias, then use nslookup to resolve both and inspect the SRV records under _msdcs.

quiz.p: Which record locates services such as domain controllers?
quiz.ex: SRV records advertise services and ports; AD relies on them.

quiz.p: A CNAME record is…
quiz.ex: CNAME aliases one name to another.

quiz.p: SPF and DKIM values are typically published as which record?
quiz.ex: Email authentication data is stored in TXT records.

content.intro: When your server can't answer a query itself, forwarding controls where it goes next — key for performance and hybrid/partner setups.

ul.t: send all unresolved queries to a specific upstream DNS (e.g. your ISP or a public resolver).
send queries for a specific domain to a specific server (e.g. a partner's DNS).
the fallback list of root servers used if no forwarder is set.

p: A recursive resolver chases a query all the way to an answer on the client's behalf. Disable recursion on internet-facing authoritative servers to reduce abuse.

note.text: Conditional forwarders are the clean way to resolve names across a forest trust or to a partner without full zone transfers.

content.practice: Configure a conditional forwarder for a fictitious partner domain 'partner.local' pointing at its DNS server IP.

quiz.p: A conditional forwarder sends queries for…
o: A specific domain to a specific server
quiz.ex: It forwards a named domain's queries to a chosen server.

quiz.p: Root hints are used when…
o: No forwarder answers — to reach the root servers
quiz.ex: Root hints provide the fallback path to the DNS root.

quiz.p: On an internet-facing authoritative server you should usually…
quiz.ex: Disabling recursion reduces abuse and amplification risk.

content.intro: DNS is a prime target and a common source of stale-record problems. These features keep it trustworthy and tidy.

p: DNSSEC signs zones so resolvers can verify answers haven't been tampered with, protecting against cache poisoning.
Dynamic records can go stale. Aging timestamps them and scavenging removes ones no longer refreshed — preventing name/IP mismatches.

ul.t: prevents cached entries being overwritten early.
mitigates amplification attacks.
only authenticated clients register records.

note.text: Enable scavenging carefully and consistently — misconfigured scavenging can delete records that are still in use.

content.practice: Enable aging/scavenging on a lab zone and describe what DNSSEC protects against in your own words.

quiz.p: DNSSEC primarily protects against…
quiz.ex: DNSSEC lets resolvers verify record authenticity, countering poisoning.

quiz.p: Scavenging is used to…
quiz.ex: Scavenging cleans up records that are no longer refreshed.

quiz.p: Which reduces DNS being used in amplification attacks?
quiz.ex: RRL limits repetitive responses used in amplification.

content.intro: DHCP hands out IP configuration automatically. A scope defines the addresses and options a server leases to a subnet.

p: Clients get an address through Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge (DORA), then hold it for the lease duration.

ul.t: the pool of leasable IPs.
addresses inside the range to skip (e.g. static devices).
a fixed IP tied to a MAC address.
gateway (003), DNS (006), domain (015), and more.

note.text: Shorter leases suit changeable networks (guest Wi-Fi); longer leases reduce traffic on stable ones.

content.practice: Create a DHCP scope for a lab subnet with an exclusion range and a reservation, and set the gateway and DNS options.

quiz.p: The DHCP lease process is abbreviated…
quiz.ex: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

quiz.p: A DHCP reservation ties an IP to a device's…
quiz.ex: Reservations bind an address to a MAC.

quiz.p: Which DHCP option delivers the default gateway?
quiz.ex: Option 003 is the router/default gateway; 006 is DNS.

content.intro: If DHCP goes down, clients eventually can't get addresses. Windows Server offers built-in ways to keep it running.

ul.t: two servers share the scope actively.
one serves; the partner takes over on failure.
two servers each own part of the range (e.g. 80/20).
groups multiple scopes on one physical network.

p: Since DHCP uses broadcasts, a DHCP relay agent (IP helper on the router/switch) forwards requests from subnets without a local DHCP server.

note.text: DHCP failover (built into modern Windows Server) is preferred over manual split-scope — it syncs leases automatically.

content.practice: In a lab with two DHCP servers, configure DHCP failover in hot-standby mode for a scope and simulate a failover.

quiz.p: DHCP failover hot-standby means…
o: One serves; the partner takes over on failure
quiz.ex: Hot standby keeps a passive partner ready to take over.

quiz.p: A DHCP relay agent is needed when…
o: Every subnet has a DHCP server
A subnet has no local DHCP server
quiz.ex: Relay agents forward DHCP across subnets that lack a local server.

quiz.p: The modern preferred HA method is…
quiz.ex: Built-in DHCP failover syncs leases automatically.

content.intro: A few checks resolve most DHCP problems — from clients with no address to duplicate IPs.

p: In a domain, a DHCP server must be authorized in AD before it will hand out leases — a safeguard against rogue servers.

ul.t: the client got no lease — check server, scope exhaustion, or relay.
a static device inside the pool without an exclusion.
expand the range or shorten leases.

note.text: Review the DHCP console's Address Leases and the server's audit logging to see who got what and when.

content.practice: On a lab client run ipconfig and interpret the result; then intentionally exhaust a tiny scope and observe a client falling back to APIPA.

quiz.p: A client showing a 169.254.x.x address means…
o: DHCP failed to assign an address
quiz.ex: 169.254 (APIPA) indicates no DHCP lease was obtained.

quiz.p: In a domain, a DHCP server must be… before it leases addresses.
quiz.ex: AD authorization prevents rogue DHCP servers.

quiz.p: A duplicate-IP conflict on the LAN often comes from…
o: A static device inside the DHCP pool without an exclusion
quiz.ex: Static IPs within the pool need exclusions to avoid conflicts.

courses.title: File & Storage Services
courses.description: Deliver reliable file services — NTFS and share permissions, DFS, quotas and file screening, Storage Spaces, iSCSI, deduplication, and shadow copies.

content.intro: File access is governed by two permission layers. Knowing how they combine prevents both lockouts and over-sharing.

ul.t: apply only over the network to the shared folder.
apply locally and over the network, at file and folder level.

p: Over the network the effective permission is the most restrictive of the share and NTFS results. Best practice: set Share to a broad level and control access precisely with NTFS.

ul: NTFS permissions inherit down the folder tree by default
Use the Effective Access tab to see a user's real result
Prefer group-based permissions over per-user

note.text: Deny overrides Allow. An accidental Deny on a group a user belongs to will block them even if another group allows it.

content.practice: Create a share where Everyone has Full Control at the share level but NTFS grants a specific group Modify — then use Effective Access to verify a user's real permission.

quiz.p: Over the network, the effective permission is…
o: The most restrictive of share and NTFS
quiz.ex: The combined result is the most restrictive of the two layers.

quiz.p: Which permission type also applies when logged on locally?
quiz.ex: NTFS permissions apply locally and over the network; share is network-only.

quiz.p: An explicit Deny…
quiz.ex: Deny takes precedence over Allow in the access check.

content.intro: Distributed File System (DFS) unifies scattered shares behind one path and keeps copies in sync across servers.

p: Presents multiple physical shares under a single logical path like \\corp\files, so users have one place to go even if data moves or lives on many servers.
Keeps folder targets synchronised between servers using efficient, block-level replication — used for redundancy and branch-office data.

note.text: DFS-N + DFS-R gives users a stable path with a nearby, replicated copy — resilient to a single server outage.

content.practice: Create a DFS namespace \\lab\files with two folder targets, then set up DFS replication between them and confirm a test file syncs.

quiz.p: DFS Namespaces provide…
o: A single logical path over multiple shares
quiz.ex: DFS-N unifies shares behind one namespace path.

quiz.p: DFS Replication is used to…
o: Keep folder copies synchronised across servers
quiz.ex: DFS-R replicates folder contents between targets.

quiz.p: A benefit of combining DFS-N and DFS-R is…
o: A stable path with a resilient, nearby copy
quiz.ex: Users keep one path while data stays replicated and available.

content.intro: FSRM adds governance to file servers — limiting consumption, blocking unwanted file types, and reporting on usage.

ul.t: limit space on a folder or volume, with soft (warn) or hard (enforce) limits.
block or warn on specific file types (e.g. .mp3, .exe).
find large, duplicate, or old files.

note.text: Soft quotas notify without blocking (good for monitoring); hard quotas prevent writes past the limit.

content.practice: Apply a 5 GB hard quota to a lab folder and a file screen that blocks executable files, then test both.

quiz.p: An FSRM hard quota…
quiz.ex: Hard quotas enforce the limit; soft quotas only warn.

quiz.p: File screening is used to…
o: Block or warn on specific file types
quiz.ex: File screens control which file types can be saved.

quiz.p: Which finds large or old files on a share?
quiz.ex: FSRM generates storage reports on usage patterns.

content.intro: Storage Spaces pools physical disks into flexible virtual volumes with software resiliency — no hardware RAID controller required.

p: You add physical disks to a storage pool, then carve out virtual disks (spaces) with a chosen resiliency and size.

ul.t: striped, no redundancy (fast, risky).
two/three-way copies survive disk loss.
space-efficient redundancy (like RAID-5), slower writes.

note.text: Tiering keeps hot data on SSDs and cold data on HDDs; thin provisioning allocates space on demand — but monitor real usage.

content.practice: In a lab with several disks, create a storage pool and a two-way mirror virtual disk, then format and share it.

quiz.p: A two-way mirror space protects against…
quiz.ex: A mirror keeps copies so it survives a disk failure.

quiz.p: Parity resiliency is best described as…
quiz.ex: Parity is space-efficient like RAID-5 but has a write penalty.

quiz.p: Storage Spaces requires…
o: Pooled physical disks and software resiliency
quiz.ex: It provides software resiliency over a pool of disks.

content.intro: iSCSI presents block storage over the network, letting servers use centralised storage as if it were a local disk — the basis for clustering.

ul.t: the server offering the storage (a LUN).
the client that connects and sees a new disk.

p: Shared block storage is what lets multiple nodes access the same disk — a requirement for failover clustering.

note.text: iSCSI runs over standard Ethernet; isolate it on its own network/VLAN for performance and security.

content.practice: Create an iSCSI target with a virtual disk on one lab server and connect to it from another using the iSCSI Initiator.

quiz.p: In iSCSI, the server offering storage is the…
quiz.ex: The target presents the storage; the initiator connects to it.

quiz.p: Shared block storage via iSCSI is a requirement for…
quiz.ex: Clustered nodes need shared storage, which iSCSI can provide.

quiz.p: For best performance, iSCSI traffic should be…
quiz.ex: Isolating iSCSI improves performance and security.

content.intro: Two features that quietly save space and save users from themselves: data deduplication and Volume Shadow Copies.

p: Dedup stores duplicate chunks once, reclaiming large amounts of space on file servers and VDI/backup volumes — often 50%+.
Volume Shadow Copies capture point-in-time versions of files on a share, so users can restore a previous version themselves via the Previous Versions tab.

note.text: Shadow copies live on the same volume — they help with accidental edits/deletes but are not a substitute for real backups.

content.practice: Enable Shadow Copies on a lab volume, edit and save a file, then restore the earlier version from the Previous Versions tab.

quiz.p: Data deduplication saves space by…
o: Storing duplicate data chunks only once
quiz.ex: Dedup keeps a single copy of repeated chunks.

quiz.p: Volume Shadow Copies let users…
o: Restore previous versions of files themselves
quiz.ex: VSS exposes point-in-time versions via Previous Versions.

quiz.p: Shadow copies are…
o: Not a substitute for real backups
quiz.ex: They live on the same volume and don't replace backups.

courses.title: Hyper-V & Virtualization
courses.description: Virtualise workloads with Hyper-V — the hypervisor, virtual switches, VM and virtual-disk configuration, checkpoints, and live migration and replication for availability and DR.

content.intro: Hyper-V is Microsoft's type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor built into Windows Server. It lets one physical host run many isolated virtual machines.

p: A type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the hardware (efficient, used in production); a type 2 runs on top of an OS (like desktop VM apps). Hyper-V is type 1.

ul: A 64-bit CPU with virtualization (Intel VT-x/AMD-V) and SLAT
Virtualization enabled in firmware/BIOS
Enough RAM and disk for the guests

note.text: After the role installs, manage hosts with Hyper-V Manager, Windows Admin Center, or PowerShell.

content.practice: Confirm a lab host supports virtualization, install the Hyper-V role, and open Hyper-V Manager.

quiz.p: Hyper-V is which type of hypervisor?
quiz.ex: Hyper-V runs directly on the hardware — type 1.

quiz.p: Which CPU feature is required for Hyper-V?
quiz.ex: Hardware virtualization plus SLAT is required.

quiz.p: After installing the role you can manage VMs with…
quiz.ex: Hyper-V Manager, Windows Admin Center, or PowerShell.

content.intro: A virtual switch connects VMs to each other and to the physical network. Choosing the right type controls what a VM can reach.

ul.t: binds to a physical NIC — VMs reach the LAN/internet.
VMs talk to each other and the host, not the physical network.
VMs talk only to each other.

p: You can tag VM traffic with VLAN IDs, and use Switch Embedded Teaming (SET) to combine NICs for bandwidth and redundancy.

note.text: Isolate management, VM, storage, and live-migration traffic — mixing them causes contention.

content.practice: Create an external and a private virtual switch, attach two VMs to the private switch, and confirm they can reach each other but not the LAN.

quiz.p: Which virtual switch type lets VMs reach the physical LAN?
quiz.ex: An external switch binds to a physical NIC for LAN/internet access.

quiz.p: A private virtual switch allows communication…
o: Only between VMs on that switch
quiz.ex: Private switches connect VMs to each other only.

quiz.p: Combining NICs on a Hyper-V host for bandwidth/redundancy uses…
quiz.ex: SET teams physical NICs behind the virtual switch.

content.intro: A well-configured VM balances performance and portability. Generation and memory choices matter most.

ul.t: legacy BIOS boot, broad OS compatibility.
UEFI, Secure Boot, faster boot — use for modern 64-bit guests.
a fixed amount assigned to the VM.
grows/shrinks between a min and max as the guest needs — improves density.

note.text: Integration services/components give the guest better performance, time sync, and clean shutdown — keep them updated.

content.practice: Create a Generation 2 VM with dynamic memory (e.g. 1–4 GB), install a guest OS, and verify integration services are running.

quiz.p: For a modern 64-bit guest you should choose…
quiz.ex: Gen 2 uses UEFI/Secure Boot and is preferred for modern guests.

quiz.p: Dynamic memory…
o: Adjusts a VM's RAM between a min and max on demand
quiz.ex: Dynamic memory scales RAM to need, improving density.

quiz.p: Integration services provide the guest with…
o: Better performance, time sync, and clean shutdown
quiz.ex: They improve guest integration with the host.

content.intro: Virtual disks are files on the host. The format and type affect performance, space, and flexibility.

p: Prefer VHDX: up to 64 TB, better resilience to power loss, and larger block sizes. VHD is legacy (2 TB limit).

ul.t: full size allocated up front — best performance.
grows as data is written — space-efficient, slight overhead.
stores only changes from a parent disk.

note.text: Pass-through disks give a VM a whole physical disk (fast) but lose portability and checkpoint support — rarely needed today.

content.practice: Create a dynamic VHDX, attach it to a VM, add data, and observe the file growing on the host.

quiz.p: The preferred modern virtual disk format is…
quiz.ex: VHDX supports up to 64 TB and is more resilient than VHD.

quiz.p: A dynamically expanding disk…
quiz.ex: Dynamic disks grow on demand, saving space.

quiz.p: A fixed virtual disk is chosen for…
quiz.ex: Fixed disks pre-allocate for best performance.

content.intro: Checkpoints capture a VM's state so you can roll back — invaluable for testing, risky in production if misused.

ul.t: uses VSS for an application-consistent, supported snapshot (default).
captures memory state too — handy in labs, not for production apps.

p: Export copies a VM (and its disks) for backup or moving to another host; import brings it back or registers it elsewhere.

note.text: Checkpoints are not backups and shouldn't be left long-term — growing differencing files hurt performance and can fill the disk.

content.practice: Take a production checkpoint of a lab VM, make a change, then apply the checkpoint to roll back.

quiz.p: The default, application-consistent checkpoint type is…
quiz.ex: Production checkpoints use VSS for supported, consistent snapshots.

quiz.p: Checkpoints should be treated as…
quiz.ex: They're short-term rollback points, not backups.

quiz.p: Exporting a VM is used to…
o: Copy it for backup or moving to another host
quiz.ex: Export packages a VM and disks for backup/migration.

content.intro: For availability and disaster recovery, Hyper-V can move running VMs between hosts and replicate them to another site.

p: Moves a running VM to another host with no downtime — used for maintenance and load balancing. Shared-nothing live migration even moves the storage too.
Clustered Hyper-V hosts restart VMs automatically on a surviving node if a host fails — true high availability.

note.text: Replica asynchronously copies a VM to another host/site for DR; you fail over if the primary is lost — with some data-loss window.

content.practice: Describe (or lab) how you'd move a running VM to another host with live migration, and when you'd use Hyper-V Replica instead.

quiz.p: Live migration moves a running VM…
quiz.ex: Live migration relocates a running VM without downtime.

quiz.p: True high availability for VMs (auto-restart on host failure) comes from…
quiz.ex: Clustering restarts VMs on a surviving node.

quiz.p: Hyper-V Replica is primarily for…
quiz.ex: Replica provides DR by copying VMs to another location.

courses.title: Server Security & Hardening
courses.description: Harden Windows Server for the enterprise — least-privilege and tiered admin, LAPS, Defender and firewall, BitLocker and Credential Guard, patching, auditing, and hardening baselines.

content.intro: Server security starts with a model, not a tool. Least privilege and administrative tiering limit how far any single compromise can spread.

ul.t: grant only the access each account needs.
remove roles, features, and services you don't use.
layered controls so one failure isn't fatal.

p: Separate admin credentials into tiers (domain controllers, servers, workstations) and never use a high-tier credential on a lower-tier machine — this stops credential theft from cascading to Domain Admin.

note.text: Use dedicated admin accounts and Privileged Access Workstations; keep Domain Admins tiny and rarely used.

content.practice: Map your admin accounts to tiers and identify one place where a Tier-0 (DC) credential is being used on a lower tier — then plan to fix it.

quiz.p: Administrative tiering primarily prevents…
o: Credential theft cascading to full domain control
quiz.ex: Tiering stops a compromised low-tier machine yielding high-tier credentials.

quiz.p: Reducing attack surface means…
o: Removing unused roles, features, and services
quiz.ex: Fewer running components means fewer things to attack.

quiz.p: Least privilege says accounts should have…
quiz.ex: Grant the minimum access required.

content.intro: A shared local Administrator password across machines is a gift to attackers. LAPS fixes it.

p: If every machine has the same local admin password, compromising one exposes them all (a lateral-movement dream).
Windows LAPS sets a unique, random local admin password per machine, rotates it automatically, and stores it securely in Active Directory (or Entra ID) where only authorised admins can read it.

note.text: LAPS is one of the highest-impact, lowest-cost hardening steps you can deploy.

content.practice: Explain how LAPS would change an incident where one workstation's local admin password is stolen.

quiz.p: LAPS solves the risk of…
o: A shared local admin password across machines
quiz.ex: LAPS gives each machine a unique, rotated local admin password.

quiz.p: LAPS stores the managed passwords…
quiz.ex: Passwords are protected in the directory for authorised readers.

quiz.p: A key benefit of LAPS is…
o: Unique, automatically rotated local admin passwords
quiz.ex: Unique rotating passwords stop lateral movement via shared creds.

content.intro: Every Windows Server ships with capable built-in protection — antimalware and a host firewall — that should be configured, not disabled.

p: Real-time protection built into the OS; on servers it integrates with Defender for Endpoint for EDR. Keep definitions current and avoid broad exclusions.

ul.t: Domain, Private, Public — different rules per network type.
inbound and outbound, by port, program, or service.

note.text: Default-deny inbound and allow only required ports — manage rules centrally with Group Policy.

content.practice: Create an inbound firewall rule allowing only a specific app/port on a lab server and confirm other inbound traffic is blocked.

quiz.p: Defender Firewall profiles (Domain/Private/Public) exist to…
o: Apply different rules per network type
quiz.ex: Profiles tailor rules to the connected network.

quiz.p: A secure default firewall stance is…
o: Default-deny inbound, allow only what's needed
quiz.ex: Default-deny with explicit allows is the norm.

quiz.p: Broad antivirus exclusions are…
o: A risk that can hide malware
quiz.ex: Excessive exclusions create blind spots for malware.

content.intro: Two protections that defend data at rest and credentials in memory — important for servers in less-controlled locations.

p: Full-volume encryption that renders a stolen disk unreadable without the key. Uses a TPM to protect keys; recovery keys should be escrowed in AD.
Uses virtualization-based security to isolate secrets (like NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets) so malware can't scrape them from memory — countering pass-the-hash.

note.text: BitLocker is especially important for branch-office servers and anything physically exposed.

content.practice: On a lab server with a TPM, enable BitLocker on a data volume and confirm the recovery key is backed up to AD.

quiz.p: BitLocker protects…
o: Data at rest on a volume
quiz.ex: BitLocker encrypts volumes so a stolen disk is unreadable.

quiz.p: Credential Guard defends against…
quiz.ex: It isolates secrets using virtualization-based security.

quiz.p: BitLocker recovery keys should be…
quiz.ex: Escrow keys in AD so admins can recover volumes.

content.intro: Unpatched servers are the most common way in. A disciplined update process closes known vulnerabilities before they're exploited.

p: Most breaches exploit known, already-patched vulnerabilities. Timely patching is the highest-value routine security work.

ul.t: approve and distribute Microsoft updates internally.
Windows Update for Business, Intune, or Configuration Manager.

note.text: Test in a ring first, schedule maintenance windows, and track compliance — patching without reporting is guesswork.

content.practice: Outline a monthly patch cycle for a lab: test ring, approval, maintenance window, and how you'd verify compliance.

quiz.p: Most breaches exploit…
quiz.ex: Timely patching closes the known holes attackers use most.

quiz.p: WSUS is used to…
o: Approve and distribute Microsoft updates internally
quiz.ex: WSUS centralises update approval and delivery.

quiz.p: A safe patch process includes…
o: Patching all servers at once with no testing
A test ring, maintenance windows, and compliance tracking
quiz.ex: Rings, windows, and reporting reduce risk.

content.intro: You can't detect what you don't log. Auditing produces the evidence for detection, investigation, and compliance.

p: Configure via Group Policy to log the events that matter — logons, account management, object access, privilege use — without drowning in noise.

ul.t: audit events on each server.
forward to a SIEM or Windows Event Forwarding for correlation.

note.text: Failed logons, new admin group members, and cleared logs are high-signal events worth alerting on.

content.practice: Enable auditing for account-management events on a lab DC, add a user to a privileged group, and find the corresponding Security log event.

quiz.p: Audit policy is best configured through…
quiz.ex: Advanced audit policy is deployed via Group Policy.

quiz.p: For correlation across many servers, forward events to…
quiz.ex: Central collection enables correlation and alerting.

quiz.p: A high-signal event worth alerting on is…
o: A user added to a privileged group
quiz.ex: Privileged group changes are security-relevant.

content.intro: Hardening is the sum of many small removals and settings. Baselines make it consistent and repeatable.

ul: Install only required roles/features
Disable legacy protocols (e.g. SMBv1)
Enable SMB signing
Turn off unused services

ul.t: guards the process holding credentials.
prefer Kerberos.

note.text: Apply Microsoft Security Baselines (via the Security Compliance Toolkit) as GPOs, then tailor — far better than hand-rolling.

content.practice: Confirm SMBv1 is removed and SMB signing is enabled on a lab server, and note two other services you could safely disable.

quiz.p: A basic hardening step is to…
quiz.ex: SMBv1 is obsolete and insecure — remove it.

quiz.p: The best way to apply consistent hardening is…
quiz.ex: Baselines give vetted, repeatable configuration.

quiz.p: Preferring Kerberos and limiting NTLM helps because…
o: NTLM is weaker and abused in credential attacks
quiz.ex: Reducing NTLM cuts exposure to credential-relay/theft attacks.

courses.title: PowerShell Automation for Windows Server
courses.description: Automate Windows Server with PowerShell — cmdlets and the object pipeline, remoting, bulk administration, scheduled reporting, and an introduction to Desired State Configuration.

content.intro: PowerShell is the automation engine of Windows Server. Everything you can do in the GUI you can script — faster, repeatably, and at scale.

p: Commands follow a Verb-Noun pattern (Get-Service, Restart-Computer, New-ADUser), which makes them discoverable and consistent.

sections.code:
Get-Command *service*
Get-Help Get-Service -Examples
Get-Member       # inspect an object's properties/methods

note.text: PowerShell passes rich objects down the pipeline, so you can filter and act on real properties — not scrape text.

content.practice: Use Get-Command, Get-Help, and Get-Member to explore the Get-Service cmdlet and list its properties.

quiz.p: PowerShell cmdlets follow which naming pattern?
quiz.ex: Cmdlets use Verb-Noun, e.g. Get-Service.

quiz.p: Which cmdlet shows an object's properties and methods?
quiz.ex: Get-Member inspects the pipeline object's members.

quiz.p: PowerShell pipelines pass…
quiz.ex: Objects flow through the pipeline, enabling property-based work.

content.intro: The pipeline is where PowerShell's power lives: select, filter, sort, and shape objects into exactly what you need.

ul.t: filter by a condition.
choose properties (columns).
order results.
count/sum/average.

sections.code:
Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq 'Running'} |
  Select-Object Name, StartType | Sort-Object Name

note.text: Format-Table/Format-List are for display only — put them at the very end, never mid-pipeline before more processing.

content.practice: Write a one-liner that lists only stopped services, showing Name and StartType, sorted by name.

quiz.p: Which cmdlet filters objects by a condition?
quiz.ex: Where-Object filters on a property test.

quiz.p: $_ in a pipeline refers to…
quiz.ex: $_ is the current object flowing through the pipeline.

quiz.p: Format-* cmdlets should be placed…
quiz.ex: Formatting is for output; keep it last.

content.intro: Day-to-day server tasks map directly to cmdlets — roles, services, logs, and configuration.

ul.t: — manage roles and features.
— control services.
— query event logs efficiently.
— inspect storage.

p: A short script applies the same change to many servers identically — no missed checkboxes, and it's self-documenting.

content.practice: Use PowerShell to list installed roles on a lab server and query the last 20 System log errors with Get-WinEvent.

quiz.p: Which cmdlet installs a server role?
quiz.ex: Install-WindowsFeature adds roles/features.

quiz.p: An efficient way to query event logs is…
quiz.ex: Get-WinEvent queries the Windows event logs.

quiz.p: Scripting a change across servers helps because it is…
quiz.ex: Scripts apply identical, repeatable, documented changes.

content.intro: Remoting runs commands on remote servers from one console — essential for managing fleets, including Server Core.

sections.code:
Invoke-Command -ComputerName SRV1,SRV2 -ScriptBlock { Get-Service DNS }
Enter-PSSession -ComputerName SRV1     # interactive

p: Remoting uses WinRM (enabled by Enable-PSRemoting). Persistent sessions (New-PSSession) let you reuse a connection for multiple commands.

note.text: Remoting is encrypted and authenticated; scope who can connect and prefer running against many servers in parallel with Invoke-Command.

content.practice: Enable remoting in a lab, then use Invoke-Command to query a service on two servers at once.

quiz.p: Which cmdlet runs a scriptblock on remote computers?
quiz.ex: Invoke-Command executes remotely, optionally in parallel.

quiz.p: PowerShell remoting relies on which protocol?
quiz.ex: WinRM underpins PowerShell remoting.

quiz.p: A persistent reusable connection is created with…
quiz.ex: New-PSSession creates a reusable remoting session.

content.intro: The real payoff is doing a hundred things at once — creating users from a spreadsheet, or applying a change across an OU.

ul.t: ForEach-Object / foreach to repeat work.
reuse logic.
try/catch with -ErrorAction Stop.

note.text: Test with -WhatIf first — it shows what a command would change without doing it. Invaluable for bulk operations.

content.practice: Write a script that reads a CSV of users and creates them in a test OU — run it first with -WhatIf.

quiz.p: Which cmdlet reads a CSV to drive bulk changes?
quiz.ex: Import-Csv turns spreadsheet rows into objects to process.

quiz.p: Before a bulk change, you should test with…
quiz.ex: -WhatIf previews changes without applying them.

quiz.p: Robust scripts handle failures with…
quiz.ex: try/catch plus -ErrorAction Stop catches and manages errors.

content.intro: Automation finishes the job when it runs on a schedule, produces reports, and enforces desired state.

p: Run scripts unattended with Task Scheduler or scheduled jobs — nightly reports, cleanup, health checks.

sections.code:
Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq 'Stopped' |
  Export-Csv stopped.csv -NoTypeInformation
# or ConvertTo-Html for a report

note.text: DSC declares the state a server should be in and corrects drift automatically — configuration as code.

content.practice: Create a scheduled task that exports stopped services to a CSV daily, and describe in one line what DSC would add.

quiz.p: Exporting results to a spreadsheet uses…
quiz.ex: Export-Csv writes objects to CSV.

quiz.p: Running a script unattended on a schedule uses…
quiz.ex: Task Scheduler runs scripts on a schedule.

quiz.p: Desired State Configuration (DSC) is best described as…
quiz.ex: DSC enforces a declared desired state, fixing drift.

courses.title: Backup, Recovery & High Availability
courses.description: Keep services running and data recoverable — backup fundamentals, Windows Server Backup, restore scenarios, failover clustering, and disaster-recovery planning.

content.intro: Backups are the last line of defence against failure, mistakes, and ransomware. A sound strategy balances how much you can lose against cost.

ul.t: everything; simplest restore, largest.
changes since the last backup; small, but restore needs the full + all increments.
changes since the last full; restore needs full + latest differential.

p: Three copies, on two media types, one offsite — so no single event takes everything.

note.text: RPO (how much data you can lose) and RTO (how fast you must recover) drive the whole design.

content.practice: For a lab file server, choose a backup schedule (full + differential vs incremental) and justify it using RPO/RTO.

quiz.p: An incremental backup captures…
o: Changes since the last backup of any type
quiz.ex: Incrementals store changes since the previous backup; restores chain them.

quiz.p: The 3-2-1 rule means…
quiz.ex: Three copies, two media, one offsite.

quiz.p: RPO defines…
o: How much data you can afford to lose
quiz.ex: RPO is the acceptable data-loss window; RTO is recovery time.

content.intro: Windows Server Backup (WSB) is the built-in tool for protecting a server, its System State, and full bare-metal images.

ul.t: data protection.
the config needed to rebuild roles like AD.
a full image to rebuild the whole server.

p: WSB can run scheduled backups to a dedicated disk or network share; keep multiple restore points.

note.text: On a domain controller, System State includes Active Directory — back it up regularly.

content.practice: Install Windows Server Backup on a lab server and configure a scheduled bare-metal + System State backup.

quiz.p: On a domain controller, System State backup includes…
quiz.ex: System State on a DC captures AD (NTDS.dit, SYSVOL, etc.).

quiz.p: A bare-metal recovery backup lets you…
o: Rebuild the entire server onto new hardware
quiz.ex: BMR restores the whole system image.

quiz.p: Windows Server Backup can target…
o: A dedicated disk or network share
Only the C: drive it backs up
quiz.ex: WSB writes to a dedicated disk or a network share.

content.intro: Backups are only proven by restores. Different failures call for different recovery methods.

ul.t: recover individual data from a backup or shadow copy.
repair a broken server configuration.
rebuild a dead server from an image.

p: To bring back deleted AD objects across the domain, boot into Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) and mark objects authoritative — or use the AD Recycle Bin for simple cases.

note.text: An untested backup isn't a backup. Schedule periodic test restores to prove your recovery works.

content.practice: Perform a file restore from a lab backup, and describe when you'd use an authoritative AD restore instead of the Recycle Bin.

quiz.p: An untested backup…
o: Isn't proven until a restore succeeds
quiz.ex: Only a successful restore proves a backup.

quiz.p: To recover deleted AD objects across the domain you can use…
o: DSRM authoritative restore or AD Recycle Bin
quiz.ex: DSRM authoritative restore (or the Recycle Bin) recovers AD objects.

quiz.p: Bare-metal recovery is used when…
o: An entire server must be rebuilt
quiz.ex: BMR rebuilds a whole failed server from an image.

content.intro: Failover clustering groups servers so that if one node fails, another takes over the workload automatically — the foundation of high availability.

p: Multiple nodes share access to storage and present clustered roles (file servers, Hyper-V VMs, SQL). If a node fails, its roles restart on a surviving node.
Quorum decides how many nodes must be available to keep the cluster running, preventing 'split-brain'. A witness (disk or cloud) helps small clusters vote.

note.text: Nodes need shared storage (e.g. iSCSI or Storage Spaces Direct) and reliable networking between them.

content.practice: Describe the nodes, shared storage, and quorum witness you'd use to make a lab file server highly available.

quiz.p: Failover clustering provides…
o: Automatic workload takeover if a node fails
quiz.ex: Clustering restarts roles on a surviving node for HA.

quiz.p: Quorum exists to…
o: Decide how many nodes must be up (avoid split-brain)
quiz.ex: Quorum keeps the cluster consistent and prevents split-brain.

quiz.p: Cluster nodes typically require…
o: Shared storage and reliable inter-node networking
quiz.ex: Shared storage and good networking are core requirements.

content.intro: High availability handles a failed node; disaster recovery handles a lost site. Planning turns a catastrophe into a procedure.

p: Agree RPO and RTO per service with the business — they justify the spend and shape the design.

ul: Offsite/second-site copies (replication or backups)
A documented, tested runbook for failover
Clear roles and communication during an event

note.text: Run DR drills. A plan that has never been exercised will fail when you need it most.

content.practice: Draft a one-page DR runbook for a critical lab service: RPO/RTO, where the copy lives, failover steps, and how you'd test it.

quiz.p: Disaster recovery (vs high availability) addresses…
quiz.ex: DR covers site-level loss; HA covers node-level failure.

quiz.p: RPO and RTO should be…
o: Agreed with the business per service
quiz.ex: The business sets acceptable loss/recovery targets.

quiz.p: A DR plan is only trustworthy if it is…
quiz.ex: Untested DR plans tend to fail in a real event.

courses.title: Foundations & Deployment
courses.description: Start strong with Windows Server — editions and licensing, Server Core vs Desktop, initial configuration, modern management tools, roles and features, and deployment at scale.

content.intro: Choosing the right edition and licensing model — and installing cleanly — sets the foundation for everything else.

ul.t: most workloads; limited virtualization rights.
highly virtualized/software-defined datacentres; unlimited VM rights.

p: Windows Server is licensed per physical core (with a minimum), plus Client Access Licenses (CALs) for users or devices that connect.

note.text: Plan disk layout (separate OS and data), set a strong local admin password, and patch immediately after install.

content.practice: Decide which edition fits a host that will run 12 VMs, and explain the licensing implication in one sentence.

quiz.p: Which edition gives unlimited virtualization rights for dense hosts?
quiz.ex: Datacenter suits highly virtualized hosts with unlimited VM rights.

quiz.p: Windows Server is primarily licensed…
quiz.ex: Core-based licensing plus CALs for connecting users/devices.

quiz.p: Client Access Licenses (CALs) are required for…
o: Users or devices connecting to the server
quiz.ex: CALs cover the users/devices that access the server.

content.intro: Windows Server installs in two flavours. The headless Server Core is smaller and more secure but changes how you manage it.

ul.t: full GUI; easiest to learn.
no desktop GUI — smaller footprint, fewer updates, smaller attack surface.

p: Configure locally with sconfig and PowerShell; manage remotely with Windows Admin Center, RSAT, or remoting.
sections.code: sconfig      # menu-driven local setup on Server Core

note.text: Prefer Server Core for infrastructure roles (DC, DNS, Hyper-V) to reduce patching and exposure.

content.practice: List two roles you'd run on Server Core and how you would manage them without a local GUI.

quiz.p: Server Core's main advantages are…
o: Smaller footprint, fewer updates, smaller attack surface
quiz.ex: No desktop shell means less to patch and attack.

quiz.p: On Server Core, quick local configuration is done with…
quiz.ex: sconfig and PowerShell configure a headless server locally.

quiz.p: Server Core is a good fit for…
quiz.ex: Its reduced surface suits core infrastructure roles.

content.intro: Every new server needs the same first steps before it does its job — identity, network, and domain membership.

ul: Set a meaningful computer name
Assign a static IP, subnet, gateway, and DNS
Set time zone and confirm time sync
Join the domain (for member servers)

p: Only after the basics are right do you install the role(s) the server exists for — keeping it minimal.

note.text: Infrastructure servers (DC, DNS, DHCP) must use static IPs — a changing address breaks the services that depend on them.

content.practice: Configure a lab member server: set its name, a static IP with the DC as DNS, and join it to the domain.

quiz.p: Infrastructure servers should use…
quiz.ex: DCs/DNS/DHCP need stable static addresses.

quiz.p: A member server's DNS should point to…
quiz.ex: Domain members must resolve via internal DNS to find the domain.

quiz.p: Roles should be installed…
o: After the basic identity and network setup
quiz.ex: Get identity and networking right first, then add roles.

content.intro: Modern Windows Server is managed centrally. Two tools cover almost everything from one place.

p: Manages local and remote servers grouped into pools — add roles, view events, and monitor status across many servers.
A browser-based tool that manages servers, clusters, and even Server Core through a modern UI — increasingly the default.

note.text: Manage servers remotely from a workstation with RSAT/WAC rather than logging on to each console — safer and faster.

content.practice: Add a second lab server to Server Manager (or WAC) and manage it remotely without signing in to its console.

quiz.p: Windows Admin Center is…
quiz.ex: WAC manages servers/clusters from a web UI.

quiz.p: Server Manager can manage…
o: Local and remote servers in pools
quiz.ex: It manages groups of local and remote servers.

quiz.p: Best practice for day-to-day admin is to…
o: Log on to each server console
quiz.ex: Remote management reduces risk and saves time.

content.intro: A server's purpose is defined by its roles. Adding only what's needed keeps it fast and secure.

ul.t: a primary function (AD DS, DNS, DHCP, Web Server).
a supporting capability (e.g. .NET, failover clustering, BitLocker).

note.text: Every extra role is more to patch and secure — install the minimum and remove what you no longer use.

content.practice: List the installed roles on a lab server with PowerShell and remove one feature you don't need.

quiz.p: A 'role' in Windows Server is…
o: A primary server function like DNS or AD DS
quiz.ex: Roles define the server's main function.

quiz.p: Which cmdlet installs roles and features?
quiz.ex: Install-WindowsFeature adds roles/features.

quiz.p: Installing only needed roles…
quiz.ex: Fewer roles means less to maintain and secure.

content.intro: Building servers one by one doesn't scale. Imaging and automation make deployments fast and identical.

p: Prepare a reference install, generalise it with Sysprep (removing unique SIDs), and capture it as an image to deploy repeatedly.

ul.t: drive an unattended install.
network-based OS deployment.
clone VMs from a golden image in virtualised environments.

note.text: Identical builds mean predictable behaviour and easier troubleshooting — avoid hand-built snowflakes.

content.practice: Outline how you'd deploy 20 identical servers: reference image, Sysprep, and the tool you'd use to push it.

quiz.p: Sysprep is used to…
o: Generalise an image (remove unique SIDs) before capture
quiz.ex: Sysprep prepares an image for reuse by removing machine-specific identity.

quiz.p: An unattended install is driven by…
quiz.ex: Answer files automate Windows setup.

quiz.p: Deploying identical images helps because it…
o: Makes behaviour predictable and troubleshooting easier
quiz.ex: Standard builds are predictable and easier to support.

courses.title: Networking & Remote Access
courses.description: Connect and extend the network with Windows Server — host networking, RRAS and VPN, RADIUS/NPS, modern Always On VPN, and Remote Desktop Services.

content.intro: Solid host networking underpins every server role — addressing, name resolution, and resilient NICs.

ul: Static IP, subnet mask, gateway on infrastructure servers
Point DNS at internal domain controllers
Verify with ipconfig /all and Test-NetConnection

p: Combine multiple NICs for bandwidth and failover so a single cable or port failure doesn't take the server offline.

note.text: Test-NetConnection checks reachability and a specific port — great for confirming a service is listening.

content.practice: Configure a static IP and test connectivity to a DC's LDAP port with Test-NetConnection.

quiz.p: Infrastructure servers should point DNS at…
quiz.ex: Domain members resolve via internal DNS to reach the domain.

quiz.p: NIC teaming provides…
quiz.ex: Teaming aggregates NICs and survives a link failure.

quiz.p: Which cmdlet tests reachability to a specific port?
quiz.ex: Test-NetConnection checks host and port connectivity.

content.intro: The Routing and Remote Access role (RRAS) turns Windows Server into a VPN gateway and router for remote users and sites.

ul.t: individual users tunnel in from anywhere.
connects whole networks (e.g. branch to HQ).

p: Common tunnels include IKEv2 and SSTP (firewall-friendly over 443). Choose based on client support and network constraints.

note.text: RRAS works, but many organisations pair it with NPS/RADIUS for policy and use Always On VPN for a modern client experience.

content.practice: Describe whether you'd use a client VPN or site-to-site VPN to connect a small branch office, and why.

quiz.p: A site-to-site VPN connects…
quiz.ex: Site-to-site links entire networks together.

quiz.p: SSTP is often chosen because it…
quiz.ex: SSTP tunnels over TCP 443, easing firewall traversal.

quiz.p: The Windows role that provides VPN/routing is…
quiz.ex: Routing and Remote Access (RRAS) provides VPN and routing.

content.intro: Network Policy Server (NPS) is Microsoft's RADIUS implementation — central authentication and authorisation for network access.

p: NPS authenticates and authorises connection requests (VPN, wireless, wired 802.1X) against AD, applying network policies.

ul.t: is this user/device allowed?
what conditions apply (time, group, health)?
logging of access.

note.text: Wi-Fi with WPA2/3-Enterprise typically uses NPS as the RADIUS server so users authenticate with their AD credentials.

content.practice: Explain how NPS would let staff connect to secure Wi-Fi using their domain accounts.

quiz.p: NPS is Microsoft's implementation of…
quiz.ex: NPS provides RADIUS authentication/authorisation.

quiz.p: WPA2/3-Enterprise Wi-Fi commonly uses NPS to…
quiz.ex: NPS authenticates enterprise Wi-Fi against AD.

quiz.p: RADIUS 'accounting' refers to…
quiz.ex: Accounting logs who connected and when.

lessons.title: Always On VPN & Modern Remote Access

content.intro: Always On VPN is Microsoft's modern replacement for DirectAccess — seamless, policy-driven remote connectivity.

p: The VPN connects automatically and transparently whenever the device has internet, so managed devices are always reachable and compliant — no user action needed.

ul: Uses IKEv2/SSTP tunnels
Deployed and configured via Intune/MDM or scripts
Integrates with NPS for policy and conditional access

note.text: DirectAccess is legacy; new deployments should use Always On VPN or cloud-native access (e.g. Entra-based).

content.practice: List two advantages of Always On VPN over asking users to manually start a VPN client.

quiz.p: Always On VPN's key user benefit is…
quiz.ex: It connects automatically without user action.

quiz.p: Always On VPN is the modern replacement for…
quiz.ex: It supersedes the legacy DirectAccess feature.

quiz.p: Always On VPN is typically deployed via…
quiz.ex: Configuration is pushed through MDM/Intune or scripting.

content.intro: Remote Desktop Services (RDS) delivers desktops and apps from the server to users anywhere — a core remote-work capability.

ul.t: runs the sessions/apps users connect to.
distributes and reconnects sessions.
secure access over HTTPS from the internet.
a portal to published apps.

p: RDS needs RD CALs (per user or device) in addition to Windows Server CALs, managed by the RD Licensing role.

note.text: Never expose RDP directly to the internet — front it with RD Gateway (443) and MFA.

content.practice: Sketch the RDS roles you'd deploy to publish an app to remote users securely, including how they reach it from outside.

quiz.p: Which RDS role secures access from the internet over HTTPS?
quiz.ex: RD Gateway tunnels RDP over HTTPS for secure external access.

quiz.p: RDS requires which extra licensing?
quiz.ex: RD CALs are needed on top of Windows Server CALs.

quiz.p: Exposing raw RDP to the internet is…
o: A serious risk — use RD Gateway + MFA
quiz.ex: Direct RDP exposure is dangerous; front it with RD Gateway and MFA.

courses.title: Monitoring & Troubleshooting
courses.description: Keep servers healthy and fix them fast — Event Viewer, Performance Monitor, services and startup, a systematic troubleshooting method, and the most common server failures.

content.intro: The Windows event logs are the first place to look when something goes wrong — and a source of proactive warnings.

ul.t: System, Application, Security, Setup.
Information, Warning, Error, Critical.

p: Custom Views filter across logs for exactly the events you care about; event forwarding centralises logs from many servers.

note.text: Note the exact time and Event ID of a failure, then look for related events just before it across logs.

content.practice: Create a Custom View on a lab server showing only Errors and Criticals from the System and Application logs in the last 24 hours.

quiz.p: Which Windows log records service and driver events?
quiz.ex: The System log holds OS/service/driver events.

quiz.p: A Custom View lets you…
o: Filter events across logs by criteria
quiz.ex: Custom Views filter to the events you care about.

quiz.p: To centralise logs from many servers you use…
quiz.ex: Event forwarding collects logs centrally for correlation.

content.intro: Performance Monitor turns 'the server feels slow' into measured evidence — and a baseline tells you what normal looks like.

p: Track CPU, memory, disk, and network counters live, or over time with Data Collector Sets.

ul.t: sustained high % Processor Time.
low available MB, high paging.
long queue lengths / high latency.
saturation or errors.

note.text: Capture a baseline when the server is healthy — you can only spot 'abnormal' if you know 'normal'.

content.practice: Create a Data Collector Set capturing CPU, memory, and disk counters on a lab server for a few minutes and review the report.

quiz.p: A performance baseline is used to…
o: Know what 'normal' looks like to spot abnormalities
quiz.ex: Baselines define normal so anomalies stand out.

quiz.p: Sustained high disk queue length usually indicates…
quiz.ex: Long disk queues point to storage as the bottleneck.

quiz.p: Long-term counter capture uses…
quiz.ex: Data Collector Sets record counters over time.

content.intro: Many 'server down' issues are really a stopped service or a failed startup. Knowing these controls resolves them quickly.

ul.t: Automatic, Automatic (Delayed), Manual, Disabled.
configure a service to restart automatically on failure.

p: Task Manager and Resource Monitor show which process is consuming CPU, memory, disk, or network right now.

note.text: A service that won't start often has a failed dependency — check the dependency tab and the System log.

content.practice: Find a stopped Automatic service on a lab server, set its recovery to restart on failure, and start it.

quiz.p: To make a service restart automatically after a crash you configure…
quiz.ex: Service Recovery actions can restart it on failure.

quiz.p: A service that won't start often has a…
quiz.ex: Check dependencies and the System log when a service won't start.

quiz.p: Which tool shows real-time per-process resource use?
quiz.ex: Task Manager/Resource Monitor show live process resource usage.

content.intro: A repeatable method beats guessing. It gets you to root cause faster and avoids making things worse.

ul: Identify the problem and its scope (who/what/when)
Establish a theory of probable cause
Test the theory — change one thing at a time
Implement the fix and verify
Document the cause and resolution

p: Narrow the problem: one server or many? one user or all? recent change? Logs and monitoring point at the layer at fault.

note.text: Change one variable at a time — changing several at once hides which fix actually worked.

content.practice: Take a fictional 'users can't reach the file server' report and write out the five methodical steps you'd follow.

quiz.p: After forming a theory of cause you should…
o: Test it by changing one thing at a time
quiz.ex: Test one variable at a time to isolate the cause.

quiz.p: The final troubleshooting step is to…
quiz.ex: Documenting closes the loop and helps next time.

quiz.p: Good isolation asks…
o: Is it one server/user or many, and what changed?
quiz.ex: Scope and recent-change questions localise the fault.

content.intro: A handful of failure patterns cover most incidents. Recognising them speeds resolution.

ul.t: failed update, disk, or boot configuration — use recovery/last known good.
logs, updates, or shadow copies filling a volume.
a runaway process or under-sized VM.
dependency or permission problem after a change.

p: On domain members, big clock drift breaks Kerberos, causing logon and access failures — check time sync first for 'random' auth errors.

note.text: After fixing, add monitoring/alerting for that condition so it's caught early next time.

content.practice: For a server that suddenly can't authenticate domain users, list the first three things you'd check and why.

quiz.p: Sudden 'random' authentication failures on domain members often trace to…
quiz.ex: Kerberos fails when clocks drift too far — check time sync.

quiz.p: A volume filling up is commonly caused by…
quiz.ex: Runaway logs/updates/shadow copies fill disks.

quiz.p: After resolving an incident you should…
quiz.ex: Alerting catches the issue earlier next time.
